title: Why is the judgment good news?
summary: The three angels' messages proclaim that "the hour of judgment has come" - in the context of the eternal gospel and a call to worship the Creator. The investigative judgment of Daniel 7 is not meant to frighten: in heaven Jesus is our Advocate, and those who believe in Him are safe.

items.comment: The first angel carries the "eternal gospel" and proclaims: "the hour of His judgment has come" - calling people to "worship Him who created." Here the judgment is set within good news, not within dread.

questions.text: What does it mean that the message about judgment is called part of the "eternal gospel" - the good news?

items.label: the "hour of judgment" is not a literal hour
items.content: "The hour of His judgment has come" (Rev 14:7) introduces a causal "because" (Greek hoti) - here is the reason for this final call of the eternal gospel to all people. The "hour" here is not a single moment or 60 minutes, but the closing period of history that precedes the "hour of harvest" (Rev 14:15) - the second coming. First comes the decision about who will be gathered; only then comes the harvest. This is a time of grace, when the gospel can still be received.

questions.text: Since the "hour of judgment" is a time of grace before the harvest, how does that change the tone of this message?

items.comment: The call goes out: "worship Him who made heaven and earth" - this is the language of creation. We worship God as Creator, and the memorial of creation is the Sabbath (cf. the study on creation).

questions.text: Why, in the hour of judgment, does the call concern precisely the worship of the Creator?

items.label: "worship the Creator" (Rev 14:7) and the sign of worship
items.content: The first angel quotes the language of the fourth commandment: "Him who made heaven and earth, the sea and the springs of water" (cf. Ex 20:11). In the hour of judgment, then, the call concerns worshiping God as Creator, whose biblical memorial is the Sabbath. This is a positive call (to true worship), not an attack on people; it stands in contrast to the false worship described further on in Rev 14. A deeper treatment of the theme of worship and God's Law is in the studies on the Sabbath and on the "little horn" (24).

items.comment: The second angel warns: "Babylon is fallen" - a symbol of religion mixed with error. This is a warning against a system of falsehood, and at the same time a call to separate from it (Rev 18:4).

questions.text: What does it mean that "Babylon" is not a place, but a spiritual condition of mixing truth with falsehood?

items.comment: The message does not end in fear, but in a portrait of God's people: "here is the endurance of the saints, who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus." Obedience here is the fruit of faith, not its price.

questions.text: How do "the commandments of God" and "the faith of Jesus" connect here - which is the source, and which the fruit?

items.comment: The call regarding Babylon is full of care, not contempt: "Come out of her, my people." God has His children even within the system of falsehood, and He calls them to Himself.

questions.text: What does it say about God that even in "Babylon" He sees "His people" and invites them out?

sections.heading: The investigative judgment: what it is really about

items.comment: Daniel sees a courtroom: the Ancient of Days takes His seat, "the books are opened." The judgment is not improvised - it rests on a record, on the truth, not on slander.

questions.text: What gives us the certainty that God's judgment rests on the facts in the "books," and not on prejudice?

items.label: the courtroom scene of Dan 7: earth and heaven by turns
items.content: The vision of Dan 7 interweaves earthly and heavenly scenes in an alternating pattern (earth: vv. 2-8; heaven: vv. 9-10; earth: vv. 11-12; heaven: vv. 13-14): the earthly parts are in prose, the heavenly in poetry. The "thrones" and the seated "Ancient of Days" show that the judgment takes place in heaven (in the Bible a throne joined with God is always a heavenly throne). After the books are opened, the "Son of Man" comes "with the clouds" to the Ancient of Days (v. 13) - an image of Christ within the courtroom scene.

items.label: the investigative judgment and the year 1844 (callback to the study on the sanctuary)
items.content: The judgment of Dan 7:9-10,22 - the "books opened" before the second coming of the Son of Man (Dan 7:13) - is linked with the "cleansing of the sanctuary" of Dan 8:14 (see study 23) and with the heavenly ministry of Christ (Heb 8-9; cf. study 18 "The Sanctuary"). This phase, begun in 1844, is at times called the "investigative judgment": it precedes the verdict, it rests on the record of one's life, and it has the character of standing up for the faithful (Dan 7:22). Linking 1844 with the high-priestly ministry is an interpretation to be confirmed at review.

items.label: the Day of Atonement as a day of judgment (type)
items.content: Adventism reads the heavenly investigative judgment as the antitype of the Old Testament Day of Atonement (Hebrew yom kippur, "day of cleansing"; Lev 16; 23:26-32). For faithful Israelites who throughout the year had made use of the sacrifices, it was a day of acquittal and cleansing, not of dread. In the same way, the chief tone of the investigative judgment is the acquittal of God's people. The Hebrew name is yom kippur. A deeper treatment of the sanctuary typology is in study 18.

items.comment: A key detail: judgment "was given in favor of the saints of the Most High." For God's people the judgment is not a threat - it is a standing up for them and a giving of the kingdom to them.

questions.text: How does the fear of judgment change when you hear that it can turn out "in favor" of believers?

items.label: "judgment in favor of the saints" (Dan 7:22)
items.content: The Aramaic expression in Dan 7:22 can be rendered as a judgment that "was given in favor of / on behalf of" the saints. This is an important emphasis: God's judgment is not first of all directed AGAINST God's people, but stands up FOR them against accusations (cf. Zech 3:1-5). That is why biblical judgment is good news for believers. The original form has been deliberately omitted here as uncertain - to be confirmed at review.

items.comment: In this courtroom we are not alone: "we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." The Judge has the face of our Advocate, who gave His life for us.

questions.text: What changes when we realize that the One who judges you is also the One who died for you?

items.label: Christ as Advocate (parakletos) against the accuser
items.content: The Greek word in 1 John 2:1 is parakletos - "one called to one's aid," a spokesman, a defense counsel in a case. At the heavenly judgment the scene is judicial: there is an accuser - "the accuser of the brothers" (Rev 12:10) - and there is an Advocate, Jesus, who intercedes for the repentant, pointing to His shed blood. The Father is the Judge, and Christ stands on the side of those being judged as their Counsel for the defense (not as their accuser).

items.label: who judges in the first phase: the Father, with Christ present
items.content: According to Dan 7, the Judge of the first phase is the "Ancient of Days" - the Father (vv. 9-10), and the call "fear God... the hour of His judgment has come" (Rev 14:7) refers to Him. Christ "does not judge" in this phase, but is present (Dan 7:13-14) as support for those whose cases are being examined: the Father-Judge and the Son-Advocate act together for the salvation of human beings. This dissolves false fear: on both sides of the table is a God who wants to save you.

items.comment: Jesus "always lives to intercede" for us - His defense is not a one-time act, but unceasing. The High Priest is at work in real time, today.

questions.text: What does it mean for daily life that Jesus "always lives" to intercede for you?

items.comment: "There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus." The judgment exists, but for those who trust in Jesus the verdict is certain - acquittal.

questions.text: What does it mean to live "in Christ" in such a way that the judgment is a hope for you, and not a fear?

items.label: justification by faith as the basis of assurance at the judgment
items.content: Assurance at the judgment does not flow from our merits, but from the righteousness of Christ credited to us, received by faith (cf. Titus 3:5-7). It is worth stressing that the message about the judgment is "in full harmony with justification by faith." That is why the investigative judgment does not undermine the assurance of salvation - it confirms it for those who abide in Christ. "Love is made complete... so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment" (1 John 4:17).

items.comment: "Who will bring a charge? God justifies. Who will condemn? Christ intercedes for us." When the highest Judge is on your side, the accuser does not have the final word.

questions.text: Whose voice usually accuses you - and what does it mean that the Judge says: "justified"?

items.label: the "judge" in the Bible is also a deliverer of the oppressed
items.content: The Hebrew "judge" (shofet) is not only one who pronounces guilt, but also a "helper," "deliverer," "savior" (cf. Judg 3:9,15), and the aim of judgment is the restoration of peace (Hebrew shalom). The oppressed cry out to God: "judge me," that is, "stand up for me, take up my defense" (Ps 7:9; 35:24; 43:1). That is why for the wronged, God's judgment is a hope: God will ultimately set right every wrong and defends the oppressed (cf. Ps 96:13; Luke 18:7-8).

items.comment: Jesus promises: whoever believes "does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life." In a sense the verdict has already been given now - on the side of life.

questions.text: How does it change your life today if the verdict "life" has already been pronounced over the believer?

items.comment: Since we have a "great High Priest," we can "approach the throne of grace with boldness." The courtroom turns out to be a throne of grace - a place we are allowed to approach with confidence.

questions.text: What would have to change in your picture of God for you to approach Him "with boldness," and not with fear?

application.text: The "hour of judgment" sounds frightening only as long as we do not know who is sitting on our side of the table. In the heavenly courtroom our Advocate is the One who died for us and who "always lives to intercede." For those who trust in Jesus, the judgment is not a verdict to fear, but an acquittal to receive - "there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ." The good news does not stop at the forgiveness of sins: it includes the assurance that when the books are opened, your Advocate has already spoken. This frees us from fear and calls us to worship the Creator with all of life.
application.challenge: Wherever the thought of God's judgment stirs up fear in you, read Rom 8:1,33-34 aloud and insert your own name. Then make one decision that will express that you worship the Creator - the One "who made heaven and earth" (Rev 14:7).
